clue.text: Mother and doctor of many years bloom

parts.note: ma is the nursery word for a mother
to doctor a result is to rig it — fix it in advance
anything of many years is old

explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' looks like an instruction to shuffle the letters beside it. It is nothing of the kind here: it is a plain verb, handing over three letters of its own.
explanation.definitionFit: bloom → MARIGOLD: a bloom is any flower in flower, and this orange garden one is a particular instance of the general word.

clue.text: Down second flipping hot drink

parts.note: a mo is a moment — 'hang on half a mo'

indicators.note: To flip something is to turn it end for end, so the two little pieces beside it are read back the way they came.

parts.note: H is the tap marked hot, and the crossword's letter for it
to drink slowly is to sip, and these three letters turn round with the H in front of them

explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping hot drink' reads as one grumble about a scalding cuppa. The three words are three separate jobs: a synonym, an abbreviation and an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Down → MOPISH: someone mopish is moping about in low spirits, which is the gloomy sense of 'down' rather than the directional one.

clue.text: Enthusiastic clique supporting Gunners

indicators.note: A support holds something up from underneath, so in a down clue the piece named beside it sits below the other.

parts.note: the Gunners are the Royal Artillery, the British Army's gun regiment
a closed little group working together is a ring

explanation.walkthrough: The Gunners are also Arsenal, which is what the football surface wants you to hear; the letters come from the regiment the nickname was borrowed from.
explanation.definitionFit: Enthusiastic → RARING: someone raring to go is straining at the leash to start, a sense of the word that now survives only in that phrase.

clue.text: Old king hides unexpected death of spiritual mentor

indicators.note: hides means the king's letters enclose the rearranged ones

parts.note: GR stands for Georgius Rex, King George, an old king

indicators.note: unexpected suggests the letters arrive in a surprising order, so they are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An elderly monarch conceals the sudden death of his religious adviser.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unexpected death of' reads as a news report, but the three words are anagram fodder, sealed between G and R.
explanation.definitionFit: A godfather sponsors a child at baptism and guides its religious upbringing, a kind of spiritual mentor.

clue.text: Conductor reducing weight of baton, saving energy

indicators.note: Saving here means 'except for', as in 'saving your presence', so the letter it points at is left out.

parts.note: reducing weight is lightening, and it arrives one letter short
E is the physicist's letter for energy, and it is the letter that goes
a baton is a slim rod carried in the hand

explanation.walkthrough: A conductor with a baton is an orchestra, and both words have been borrowed from the wrong trade: the conductor is electrical and the baton is only a stick.
explanation.definitionFit: Conductor → LIGHTNING ROD: it carries a strike safely down to earth, so 'conductor' is meant in the electrical sense, not the musical one.

clue.text: Extreme mutt's barking outside back of Tesco

indicators.note: Barking is British slang for barking mad, and letters that have gone mad will not stay in the order they were given.
What is outside something wraps around it, so the rearranged letters open up and take the single one into the middle.

parts.note: the dog's own five letters are the raw material, apostrophe and all

indicators.note: The back of a word is the letter at its end, the one you reach last.

parts.note: Tesco is a British supermarket chain, and only its final letter is wanted

explanation.walkthrough: The surface has a dog yapping behind a shop. Nothing is barking except the letters, and the supermarket is there to give up one character.
explanation.definitionFit: Extreme → UTMOST: doing your utmost is going as far as you possibly can, and 'extreme' names that same far end of a scale.

clue.text: Feel OK, when nothing is fine

indicators.note: when, read with is, sets up a swap inside the letters OK
is, read with when, says the letter for nothing becomes the word for fine

parts.note: taken as written
O, the figure zero, stands for nothing
fine can mean thin, as a fine thread

explanation.surface: Someone reports feeling fine, as long as nothing much is going on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when nothing is fine' reads as a mood, but it is an instruction: where OK has the O for nothing, write the word for fine.
explanation.definitionFit: To feel can mean to hold an opinion, which is to think.

clue.text: Check right after crossing

parts.note: once can mean as soon as: 'once we've eaten' is right after we've eaten
to get over a river is to cross it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Right' begs to be the usual single letter for right. It belongs with 'after' instead, and both halves of this answer are ordinary words rather than abbreviations.
explanation.definitionFit: Check → ONCE-OVER: giving something the once-over is running your eye over it quickly, which is an inspection rather than a repair.

clue.text: Naturally good books accepted by story editor

indicators.note: Something accepted by others is taken in among them, so the pair of letters settles between the two pieces rather than after them.

parts.note: a story told is a tale
ED is the standing abbreviation for an editor, as printed on a masthead
the books a crossword means are usually scripture: NT is the New Testament

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a tidy scene in a publishing office, and every word of it is really shorthand — three stock abbreviations laid end to end with one tucked inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Naturally good → TALENTED: a talent is an ability you were born with, so being good at something without being taught is exactly what the word names.

clue.text: Yearly grub in batter for model

parts.note: PA is per annum, the yearly rate quoted on a savings ad

indicators.note: A piece that goes in something is buried inside it, so the digging happens within the other word rather than after it.

parts.note: to batter a door down is to ram it
to grub about in the soil is to dig

explanation.walkthrough: 'Grub in batter' sounds like something fried at a fairground. Both words are verbs here, and neither has anything to do with food.
explanation.definitionFit: model → PARADIGM: a paradigm is the pattern everything else is measured against, so 'model' means exemplar rather than a scale replica.

clue.text: Dealing with revenue approximately on island in Florida

indicators.note: In an across clue one thing sitting on another comes after it, so these two letters follow rather than lead.

parts.note: FL is the two-letter postal code for Florida, and it opens up in the middle

indicators.note: What is in something goes inside it, so everything named before lands between the two letters named after.

parts.note: IS is how an island is labelled on a map
ca. is circa, the 'approximately' put in front of a date

explanation.walkthrough: Florida does two jobs at once: it holds the holiday surface together and, split in half, it holds the wordplay too.
explanation.definitionFit: Dealing with revenue → FISCAL: fiscal matters are those concerning public money and taxation, so the adjective covers anything on the revenue side.

clue.text: Piano maker half polishes piano, preferring one side

parts.note: P is the musical abbreviation for piano, meaning soft
an artisan is a skilled maker

indicators.note: half means only the first half of the word for polishes is kept

parts.note: shines means polishes
P again, the musical abbreviation for piano

explanation.surface: A piano-maker gives one side of the instrument a better polish than the other.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a craftsman with a piano; both pianos are just P, at either end.
explanation.definitionFit: Partisanship is bias in favour of one party or faction, the state of preferring one side.

clue.text: Princess first in salon, back for quick Brazilian

indicators.note: First in a word is its opening letter, so only one character of what follows is taken.
An across entry read back runs right to left, so what has just been spelled out is written the other way.

parts.note: the Princess Royal, Anne, is the crossword's standing princess
the salon gives up its opening letter and nothing else

explanation.walkthrough: 'Quick Brazilian' sounds like a beauty treatment booked at that salon. It is a person: Ayrton, three-time Formula One world champion, killed at Imola in 1994.
explanation.definitionFit: quick Brazilian → SENNA: the definition names a driver by nationality and speed rather than by name, so it works as a definition by example.

clue.text: Find curtain rail on the floor

parts.note: the rail a curtain runs along is a curtain track
a boxer on the floor is down

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are so ordinary that the join hides in plain sight — there is no indicator anywhere to say two everyday words are being laid end to end.
explanation.definitionFit: Find → TRACK DOWN: to track something down is to find it by following its trail, so the definition is the hunting sense of the verb.

clue.text: Shifting last of crops, harvest mice stocking up then?

definitions.note: The definition is not a synonym but a date named by the thing done on it, and 'then?' is the setter admitting as much.

indicators.note: Crops being shifted are carted off somewhere else, and these letters move just as far from where they started.
The last of a word is its final letter, the one left when everything before it is taken away.

parts.note: the final letter of crops, taken on its own
eleven letters handed over whole, to be rearranged around that S

explanation.walkthrough: Harvest mice hoarding for winter is a perfectly good picture of autumn, and it is made entirely of letters: the night it points to is months later.
explanation.definitionFit: stocking up then? → CHRISTMAS EVE: it is the one night of the year stockings are hung up, so the date is defined by its own ritual.

clue.text: Archer quickly comprehends flight technology

indicators.note: To comprehend something is to take it in, and here that is meant literally: one word swallows another whole.

parts.note: to move apace is to move quickly, and the word opens up after its first letter
Eros, the god of love, does his work with a bow and arrow

explanation.walkthrough: 'Archer' looks like a surname — the novelist, or the radio family. It is the archer of Piccadilly Circus, the arrow-shooting god.
explanation.definitionFit: flight technology → AEROSPACE: the aerospace industry builds aircraft and rockets, so the phrase names a whole field of engineering rather than one machine.

clue.text: Returned to power, Labour's leader admitted requirement to fix potholes

parts.note: an MP returned at an election is back in the House

indicators.note: Somebody admitted has been let in, so the single letter goes inside the assembly rather than in front of it.

parts.note: the leader of a word is its first letter, and the party's is L
the top of an organisation is where its power sits

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is election night — in Britain a candidate is 'returned' when elected — and the answer is what a council spreads on the road afterwards.
explanation.definitionFit: requirement to fix potholes → BLACKTOP: blacktop is the asphalt a road is surfaced with, so it is literally what the hole gets filled with.

clue.text: Close friend cheers up, parting eventually

indicators.note: parting means splitting something in two, so the reversed thanks goes into the middle of the phrase for eventually

parts.note: eventually means in time, sooner or later

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word is read from the bottom, so ta is turned round

parts.note: ta and cheers are both informal British ways of saying thank you

explanation.surface: A close friend raises a toast and, in the end, the two go their separate ways.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Close friend' reads as one phrase, but 'Close' alone is the adjective sense and the pair is the noun sense. 'up' works only because this is a down clue; ta is British slang for thanks.
explanation.definitionFit: An intimate, used as a noun, is a person you are very familiar with, a confidant or bosom companion.

clue.text: Record holder with most titles?

definitions.meaning: the surface offers an athlete who holds a world record; read the other way it is an office whose job is holding records
titles here are not championships won but legal titles — the documents proving who owns a piece of ground

explanation.walkthrough: There is nothing to take apart: the whole clue is one sentence read twice, sport on the surface and property law underneath.
explanation.definitionFit: Record holder with most titles? → LAND REGISTRY: the state body keeps every registered title to property in England and Wales, so it out-titles any athlete.

clue.text: Announce that woman's hairless except head

parts.note: what belongs to that woman is hers, and the possessive gives three letters

indicators.note: Except marks what is being left out, so the letter it points at never joins the rest.

parts.note: a head with no hair on it is bald
the head of a word is its opening letter, and this is the one that comes off

explanation.walkthrough: 'Hairless except head' sounds like a description of where the hair still is. It is an instruction: take a word and knock the front off it.
explanation.definitionFit: Announce → HERALD: to herald something is to proclaim its arrival in advance, the verb behind the noun for a royal messenger.

clue.text: Monsieur's ready with a kiss — potentially gross?

parts.note: Monsieur signals French, and prêt is the French for ready
the clue's own word, taken at face value
X is the kiss pencilled at the bottom of a letter

explanation.walkthrough: 'Ready' is also slang for cash, which keeps the money surface running. And 'gross' is the accountant's word for the whole amount, not a verdict on the kiss.
explanation.definitionFit: gross → PRE-TAX: gross pay is the figure before any deductions, so a pre-tax amount and a gross one are the same number.

clue.text: Bristly feature next to private dining area?

parts.note: the part of a face that grows stubble
waiting at the door is waiting next to it, so one little word swaps for the other
your own room is your private one

explanation.walkthrough: Three ordinary words run together with no indicator anywhere, and the question mark is the setter conceding that the definition is a district, not a room.
explanation.definitionFit: dining area? → CHINATOWN: the quarter is where a city's Chinese restaurants cluster, so it is defined by what visitors mostly go there to do.

clue.text: A little cyclist pedalled around showing proficiency

indicators.note: A little of something is a small piece of it taken just as it stands, so an unbroken run of the letters that follow is what is wanted.
To go around is to come back the way you came, so the letters are picked up in the opposite direction.

parts.note: five consecutive letters straddle the gap between these two words, and they are read from right to left

explanation.walkthrough: 'A little cyclist' is not a comment on anybody's height: 'a little' means a small piece of what follows, which is where the letters are sitting.
explanation.definitionFit: showing proficiency → ADEPT: someone adept at a job does it with practised skill, so the definition describes the person rather than the work.

clue.text: Pipe down keel's centre runs straight down

parts.note: sh is the noise you make telling somebody to be quiet

indicators.note: The centre of a word is what sits at its middle, equally far from either end — here two letters of four.

parts.note: the middle pair of a four-letter word
R is runs on a cricket scorecard

explanation.walkthrough: Every word here sounds nautical — pipes, keels, running straight down — and the pieces turn out to be a hush, two middle letters and a cricket abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: straight down → SHEER: a sheer cliff drops vertically with nothing to break the fall, which is the vertical sense rather than the 'utter' one.

clue.text: Extent of movement beginning to trouble composer

indicators.note: The beginning of a word is its opening letter, and that is all the word after it gives up.

parts.note: the opening letter of the word, and no more of it
Maurice Ravel, the French composer of Boléro

explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the engineer's word, not the holiday one: the travel of a lever or a piston is how far it can move.
explanation.definitionFit: Extent of movement → TRAVEL: a mechanic calls the distance a part can move its travel, a technical use of an everyday word.

clue.text: Long trousers affected Ashe's game

indicators.note: trousers as a verb means pockets, so the word for long takes the other letters inside it

parts.note: to long for something is to pant for it

indicators.note: affected means disturbed or worked upon, so the tennis player's name is rearranged

parts.note: the name Ashe supplies the letters; the 's is read as 'is', joining the wordplay to the definition

explanation.surface: Arthur Ashe, the tennis player, is seen in long trousers, which altered his game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trousers' looks like clothing but is a verb: PANT pockets HEAS, the rearrangement of ASHE that 'affected' signals. Game here means animals hunted for sport.
explanation.definitionFit: The pheasant is a bird shot for sport, and such hunted creatures are called game.

clue.text: Nice to see motorbike race in quarry

indicators.note: A piece that goes in something drops inside it, splitting the other word apart rather than joining it at either end.

parts.note: the quarry of a hunt is the creature being chased — its prey
the TT is the Isle of Man Tourist Trophy, raced on public roads

explanation.walkthrough: The capital N is only there because the clue starts, so 'Nice' is the plain adjective rather than the French city, and 'quarry' is an animal rather than a pit.
explanation.definitionFit: Nice → PRETTY: 'a nice view' and 'a pretty view' say the same mild, pleasant thing, which is the everyday sense of both words.

clue.text: A writer Richard's mentioned added pages

indicators.note: mentioned means the word is said aloud and spelt by its sound

parts.note: A, plus pen for writer, plus Dick's, Dick being a familiar form of Richard: said together they make the answer's sound

explanation.surface: A writer called Richard is credited in some extra pages.
explanation.walkthrough: Say A, PEN (a writer) and DICK'S (Richard's) together and they sound like the answer, which is spelt differently.
explanation.definitionFit: An appendix is supplementary matter added at the end of a book, so it means added pages.
